doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: Blue Crescent, playing with Robinson and Kidd Jordan
summary: White lost his home in Katrina, wrote songs at Studio in the Woods, recorded Blue Crescent, and found the avant garde let him express feelings that tradition could not. White recalls an intuitive first concert with Robinson and sitting in with Kidd Jordan, whose listening to ambient sounds shaped his composing.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: to get back to some state of normalcy, or living in the new existence. It was very painful. There were a lot of losses. I went through a plethora of emotions: bewilderment, anger, you know of being frightened, fear. Little joy here and there. And I needed to express those things. I wrote a bunch of songs at a artist’s retreat here called Studio in the Woods, A Studio in the Woods. And I recorded them on a recording called “Blue Crescent.” And the idea was it was kind of like my version of the state of New Orleans post-Katrina. Most of the songs ended up being uptempo or nostalgic, optimistic and hopeful. There’s only one song that’s really kind of sad, it’s called “Katrina.” I can’t even play it it’s that sad. But what I found is that even with all of those new songs that I wrote, there was still feelings that I wasn’t able to express in traditional music. And I found with the avant garde I could scream, I could shout, I could curse, I could question in ways that I couldn’t in conventional musical forms. And so I continued with that, and most people, even a lot of the musicians have no idea that I do that. It’s like a secret. It has to be a secret because most people hate it. But you know I learned a lot from Perry Robinson. We played this concert and, you know, we walked out, I’d just met the musicians five minutes before. We walked out on the stage. He says, he wrote out one line and he said, “We’re going to play this in harmony, you play this part I play that and then we’ll take off from there.” And I’m thinking we’re going to do a concert and this is all we have is one line? You know. And then we walked out on the stage and he said, “Look, let’s just do the first song just the two clarinets together.” And I’m like – he said, “I’ll play something and then you answer and then we’ll meet in the middle.” And I was like, what could I say? So he started playing and I started playing, and something happened. It was something spiritual that happened and we connected and it was really beautiful in a different kind of way from what I’m used to. And I went with it. So ever since, I mean every now and then in my daily compositions something’ll come out that’s avant garde sounding and I’ll write out a line or two and use those as points of departure. But the problem is of course it's hard to find community here in that. It’s not going to be a lucrative endeavor. Jazz clubs and stuff wouldn’t want that. You know I would have to have a special concert to be able to play that music. So I’d need to find people that are interested. It’s very unfortunate that I wasn’t able to really hook up with Kidd Jordan before he passed. You know near the end I sat in with him a couple of times, like in Chicago at the Chicago Jazz Fest. He played at this club, you know, and I played with a bunch of other people, and it was great. And there were a couple of times I was able to do that. But I learned a lot from that. I mean you know Kidd’s concept of listening to sounds around you certainly has become a part of my artistic composition style. You know people would laugh and say, “Oh Kidd would make a song off the sound of the air conditioner.” You know and everybody thought that was crazy and funny and all of that.
